text: So when people say the University of Chicago was founded in 1890, they mean the second one.
At its last meeting, the old board renamed itself the Old University of Chicago, on purpose, so the new Baptist school could take the name with no legal strings attached.
There would be no shared debt, no shared trustees, no shared anything.
The new institution wanted a fresh start, and it had the money to buy one.
That money came from one man.
Rockefeller pledged six hundred thousand dollars toward a new university in Chicago.
By that point his Standard Oil controlled around ninety percent of the oil refining in the United States.
He was, by most measures, the richest man in the country.
He was also a devout Baptist, and the Baptists had wanted a great university in the Midwest for years, a flagship to match the older eastern schools.
But Rockefeller did not simply write a check.
Other donors had to come up with four hundred thousand more before his money was good.
It was a dare as much as a gift.
The American Baptist Education Society went out and raised the four hundred thousand.
With the match in hand, the University of Chicago incorporated in 1890.

Marshall Field, who owned the great department store on State Street, gave the first ten acres of land in Hyde Park, six miles south of downtown, fronting the Midway Plaisance between two parks that Frederick Law Olmsted had laid out.
The campus would rise on the blocks from 57th to 59th Street, between Ellis and Woodlawn.
